headline: Growing Number of People Fear They're 'NPC in Someone Else's Life'
subheadline: Existential concern that they exist only to advance others' storylines
summary: A new existential anxiety involves the fear that one is not the main character of reality but merely a background figure.
content:
Mental health professionals are documenting a rise in what patients describe as "NPC anxiety": the fear that they're not the main character of their own life, but rather a non-playable character in someone else's story.

The term, borrowed from video games where NPCs exist only to serve the player's narrative, has become a framework for existential dread.

"Sometimes I feel like I only exist to give other people directions," explained one sufferer. "Or to have a two-line conversation that advances their plot. Then they walk away and I just... stand here. Until the next person needs something."

The anxiety often manifests in social situations. Sufferers report feeling like their presence at events is "to fill the background" and that their conversations are "scripted" rather than meaningful.

"I went to a party," reported another individual. "I had three conversations. All of them were me giving advice or information. No one asked about my life. I was a quest-giver. I was an NPC giving quests."

Psychologists attribute the phenomenon to increased awareness of narrative structures in media, combined with social media's tendency to frame certain people as "main characters" while others fade into obscurity.

"The internet has created main characters and supporting cast," noted Dr. James Chen. "When you see influencers living cinematic lives and compare them to your routine existence... the NPC framework becomes uncomfortably apt."

Symptoms include questioning whether one's thoughts are "original" or "pre-programmed," feeling that daily routines are "loops," and existential panic when asked "what do you do for fun" and having no answer.

"What if I only have, like, four dialogue options?" one patient asked. "What if I'm repeating the same lines over and over and I don't even notice?"

Treatment focuses on recognizing that feeling like an NPC doesn't mean being one. "Unless," Dr. Chen added, then stopped himself. "No. Definitely not. Everyone is real. I'm sure of it."
author: Chris Patterson, Human Interest
